Étant donné `.claude/rules/tui-tables.md`, quand la story est livrée, alors la Rule 125 (ou une nouvelle règle) énonce que la première colonne d'une vue à opération longue est la pastille, que la couleur dit l'état et pas le type d'opération, et pas de vert pour « terminé », avec le renvoi au test garde-fou.
369	3. Étant donné la Rule 139 et la Rule 128, quand elles sont relues, alors elles renvoient à la pastille pour le cas des spinners de ligne.
370	4. Étant donné `docs/architecture/configuration.md`, quand la story est livrée, alors le réglage « sans mouvement » y est documenté (A-02).
371	5. Étant donné `docs-site/docs/reference/`, quand la story est livrée, alors la légende des glyphes y figure.
372	6. Étant donné `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, quand la story est livrée, alors sa carte d'architecture mentionne le composant et le mémorisateur.
373	
374	**Hors périmètre** : la documentation des vues non migrées.
375	
376	---
377	
378	## Questions ouvertes
379	
380	Rien ci-dessous n'est tranché ; la recommandation du PM, quand il y en a une, est une proposition. Les décisions déjà prises sont dans `brief.md`.
381	
382	1. **Vue pilote** (A-06). Recommandation: `:jobs` (déjà une colonne de glyphe, un spinner fourni par le routeur, un registre). Alternative: `ws`, plus exposée mais sans état d'échec aujourd'hui.
383	2. **Issue d'un no-go** (A-06). Si le clignotement déplaît à l'usage : glyphe statique partout, ou arrêt du chantier ?
384	3. **Glyphes et rôles de couleur** (A-01), à choisir avec le ux-designer : glyphe par état (rouge et orange doivent différer par le glyphe), glyphe de l'état « en file » dans `:jobs`, rôles surchargeables par thème (`icon_*`) ou aliases fermés.
385	4. **Priorité entre opérations simultanées sur une ligne** (A-01). Quelle opération et quel état l'emporte (par exemple en cours avant erreur, ou l'inverse) ; que dit le footer.
386	5. **Nom, portée et forme du réglage « sans mouvement »** (A-02) : global ou par contexte, valeurs, variable d'environnement, bascule à chaud par touche.
387	6. **Fréquence du tick** (A-03) : 1 Hz ou 2 Hz ; **périmètre du test « un seul tick »** : les pastilles seulement, ou aussi les spinners de chargement global du footer, qui ont leur propre chaîne ; la chaîne actuelle du routeur (D5) est-elle remplacée par le tick lent.
388	7. **Identité de la cible entre vues** (A-04) : chemin de dépôt pour `ws` et `:sec`, mais image pour OCI ; une même image et un même dépôt sont-ils la même cible ; quels types d'opération participent (scan seulement, ou aussi sync, clone, pull) ; un échec de sync dans `ws` apparaît-il dans `:sec`.
389	8. **Footer par ligne** (A-05) : la cause d'une erreur est-elle de niveau `Status` (sans minuteur) ou `Error` (rouge, 3 s) ; que montre-t-il pour plusieurs opérations simultanées.
390	9. **Colonne `Scanned`** (A-08, A-09) : que montre-t-elle pendant un scan (vide, tiret, ancien horodatage grisé, texte) pour ne pas afficher un ancien « 3 days ago » trompeur.
391	10. **Pastille sous le curseur** : le clignotement continue-t-il sur la ligne sélectionnée ? La couleur n'est pas portée sous une sélection colorée en entier ; le glyphe doit alors suffire.
392	11. **Conteneur `exited` avec le code 0** (A-14) : rouge comme `dead` (défaut actuel), orange ou dim ; `restarting` clignote-t-il alors qu'il s'agit d'un état observé.
393	12. **`:agent-usage`** (A-13) : la coloration du coût appartient-elle à ce chantier ; l'icône de type d'agent exige une seconde colonne, contraire à « pas de nouvelle colonne » (abandon, ou exception) ; référence du seuil de coût ; état de livraison de S-09 (DEVDESK-97).
394	13. **Échec de test réseau** (A-12) : résultat de ligne ou échec d'opération mémorisé.
395	14. **Vues hors inventaire** (A-00) : dashboard, status, filebrowser, viewer en suivi, setup, auth forge : migrées, hors lot, ou sans objet ?
396	15. **Remplacer l'icône de ligne pendant l'opération** (H5) : le type de la ligne (dépôt, dossier, image) est-il toujours reconnaissable sans icône ? À observer sur le pilote.
397	16. **Découpage des PR** : une PR par story (recommandation du PM) ou regroupement des vues Should ; les efforts S / M / L sont à faire valider par l'architect, et A-10 (L) à redécouper.
398	17. **Mention de l'item DEVDESK-99** : le clore dès la création de A-13, ou à sa livraison.
399	
400	Note de méthode : `research.md` ne contient pas de section de critique distincte de la recherche ; les risques de `brief.md` viennent de la liste transmise avec l'idée et des conclusions de la recherche.

1	# Indicateur d'activité uniforme (pastille en première colonne) — recherche
2	
3	Date : 2026-11-06. Légende : **[fait]** sourcé, **[estimation]** déduction signalée, **[aucune donnée]** non trouvé.
4	Limite : recherche web rapide (une passe). Plusieurs points sur les outils concurrents n'ont pas pu être vérifiés ; ils sont marqués.
5	
6	## Synthèse
7	
8	1. Aucune source trouvée ne montre un outil TUI avec une pastille **clignotante** par ligne. Les outils trouvés signalent l'état par la **couleur** (oxker) ou un **spinner** ; pour les autres (k9s, lazygit, btop, lazydocker, dry, `gh`), **[aucune donnée]** vérifiée.
9	2. Le clignotement automatique de plus de 5 s est une exigence d'accessibilité WCAG 2.2.2 (niveau A) : il faut un moyen de le mettre en pause/arrêter. WCAG vise le web, mais c'est la référence documentée la plus proche. L'application à un terminal est une **[estimation]**.
10	3. Le clignotement matériel (SGR 5) est volontairement ignoré ou désactivable dans beaucoup de terminaux ; on ne peut pas compter dessus.
11	4. La couleur seule ne doit pas porter l'information (WCAG 1.4.1) : la pastille rouge/orange doit être doublée (glyphe différent ou texte dans le footer).
12	5. Conclusion : approche **plausible mais non éprouvée ailleurs** ; le risque vient surtout du clignotement et de la couleur seule, pas de la pastille elle-même (voir §4).
13	
14	## 1. Comment les autres montrent l'activité par ligne
15	
16	| Outil | Ce qui est établi | Source |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| oxker (TUI Docker) | **[fait]** Couleur par état de conteneur : mort/sorti rouge, en pause jaune, redémarrage vert clair, running sain vert, running non sain orange (#FFB224). Pas de clignotement mentionné. | docs.rs oxker 0.13.0 config.toml |
19	| k9s | **[fait]** Les skins définissent des couleurs de statut (new/modify/add/error, pending/completed). **[aucune donnée]** sur un clignotement ou une pulsation par ligne. | k9scli.io/topics/skins |
20	| lazygit, btop, lazydocker, dry, `gh run watch` | **[aucune donnée trouvée]** (les recherches n'ont rien renvoyé d'exploitable ; à vérifier dans le code ou la doc de chacun). | — |
21	| Claude Code | **[fait]** Des issues demandent un compteur / des états par sous-agent (running, idle, completed) dans la status line, et un bug rapporte un sous-agent terminé affiché « running » indéfiniment. **[aucune donnée]** confirmant une pastille native par agent. Les outils tiers claude-hud et Fleet (tmux) montrent des pastilles de couleur par agent (vert prêt, bleu idle). | github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/27916 ; claudeissues.com/issue/32858 ; claudeissues.com/issue/40928 ; awesome.ecosyste.ms (nicknisi/fleet) |
22	| GitHub (web) | **[fait]** Primer : l'animation rassure sur l'activité mais peut distraire ; les indicateurs doivent rester discrets (pages drafts). **[aucune donnée]** officielle sur les icônes exactes des checks. Un projet tiers fait tourner les icônes en cours et coupe l'animation en reduced-motion. | primer drafts « ui-patterns/loading » ; github.com/Kilo-Org/cloud/pull/5882 |
23	
24	Leçon **[estimation]** : le motif « couleur = état » est courant (oxker) ; le motif « pastille animée par ligne » n'apparaît dans aucune source trouvée. Le risque de rupture avec les usages est donc réel mais non mesuré.
25	
26	## 2. Clignotement en terminal : accessibilité, coût, réseau
27	
28	- **[fait]** WCAG 2.2.2 : tout contenu qui clignote, démarre automatiquement, dure plus de 5 s et accompagne d'autre contenu doit pouvoir être mis en pause, arrêté ou masqué. Source : https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pause-stop-hide
29	- **[fait]** WCAG 2.3.1 : pas plus de 3 flashs par seconde (seuil d'épilepsie photosensible). Les deux critères se cumulent. Source : https://ictbaseline.access-board.gov/document-baselines/09FlashingDocs/
30	- **[fait]** Le clignotement SGR 5 est jugé gênant/inaccessible par beaucoup de terminaux, qui ne l'implémentent pas ou offrent un réglage pour le couper (iTerm2, Konsole, Terminal.app cités). Windows Terminal : débat sur le rendu « DEC » (caractères atténués) contre « PC ». Sources : https://terminfo-dev.pages.dev/sgr/5-blink ; https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/issues/7388 ; https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/issues/16753
31	- **[fait]** Un clignotement émis par l'application (alternance de glyphe/couleur à chaque tick) ne dépend pas de SGR 5, donc ne peut pas être coupé par le réglage du terminal. Déduit de ce qui précède : **[estimation]**.
32	- **[fait]** Bubble Tea : le renderer est plafonné (`WithFPS`), le spinner avance via `tea.Tick` à son propre intervalle (ex. 1/10 s, 1/8 s), `TEA_TRACE` mesure le rendu. Sources : mintlify.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/advanced/performance ; sources.debian.org (bubbles 0.21.0 spinner.go).
33	- **[aucune donnée]** mesurant le coût de redessin ou la bande passante d'un tick de pastille par ligne sur SSH/liaison lente. À mesurer sur DevDesk avec `TEA_TRACE`. Un spinner existe déjà dans `:jobs` et `:sec`, donc le coût marginal d'une pastille sur le même tick est probablement faible **[estimation]**.
34	- **[aucune donnée]** sur un équivalent de `prefers-reduced-motion` pour terminal. Le web a cette media query ; aucune convention terminal trouvée (NO_COLOR concerne la couleur, pas le mouvement). Un réglage de contexte DevDesk serait à définir (**[estimation]**).
35	- **[fait]** WCAG 1.4.1 : la couleur ne doit pas être le seul moyen de transmettre l'information ; ajouter forme ou texte. Source : https://w3c.github.io/wcag/understanding/use-of-color
36	
37	## 3. Alternatives au clignotement
38	
39	Toutes **[estimation]** de conception, à valider ; aucune source ne les compare.
40	
41	| Option | Pour | Contre |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| Spinner braille (déjà utilisé) | Familier, mouvement continu net, déjà dans le code | Plus agité qu'un clignotement lent ; occupe un glyphe mobile |
44	| Pulsation de teinte (dégradé sur 3-4 niveaux) | Plus doux qu'un on/off, reste sous 3 flashs/s | Exige du truecolor ; rendu variable selon le terminal ; plus de rafraîchissements |
45	| Glyphe alterné lent (ex. ● / ○ à ~1 Hz) | Ne repose pas sur la couleur seule ; sous le seuil des 3 flashs/s | C'est encore un clignotement : WCAG 2.2.2 s'applique au-delà de 5 s |
46	| Glyphe statique par état (● en cours, ✖ échec, ◐ idle) | Aucun mouvement, aucun coût de redessin, accessible | L'activité en cours se voit moins ; on ne distingue pas « bloqué » de « en cours » sans le footer |
47	
48	Un réglage permettant de passer en mode statique (ou de couper le mouvement) couvrirait 2.2.2 pour les options animées **[estimation]**.
49	
50	## 4. Conclusion
51	
52	- Pastille + couleur = état : courant (oxker) et cohérent avec la règle existante de DevDesk (couleur sémantique). **Faible risque**.
53	- Animation de la pastille : **non attestée** ailleurs dans ce que j'ai pu vérifier, et soumise à WCAG 2.2.2 si elle dépasse 5 s. **Risque moyen**, atténuable (réglage « sans mouvement », fréquence ≤ ~1 Hz, glyphe qui change en plus de la couleur).
54	- Couleur seule pour rouge/orange : **risque d'accessibilité** (1.4.1) ; prévoir un glyphe distinct par état et le détail dans le footer (déjà prévu).
55	- Remplacer l'icône de ligne (image/dossier/dépôt) : perte temporaire de l'information de type de ligne, à noter dans la décision ; la règle 125 (colonne d'icône sans titre, 2 cellules) reste compatible **[estimation]**.
56	
57	## Points ouverts
58	
59	- Vérifier directement le code/la doc de k9s, lazygit, btop, lazydocker, dry, `gh` (aucune donnée obtenue).
60	- Mesurer le coût de redessin sur SSH (`TEA_TRACE`).
61	- Choisir le comportement par défaut (animé ou statique) et son réglage.
62	- La pastille est-elle visible sous la ligne sélectionnée (règle 125 : la couleur disparaît sous le curseur) ?

375	## A shortcut that does not apply is greyed, not dropped
376	
377	`shortcut.Shortcut.Disabled` (§3.48). The entry keeps its place and the key
378	loses its colour and its weight, so the column no longer re-orders itself as the
379	cursor moves — which is what it is for: it is read out of the corner of the eye,
380	and a list that rearranges under the gaze cannot be.
381	
382	**A mode still replaces the list.** A form has different keys from a table, so
383	greying them would show the union of every mode. What is greyed is a *state*
384	inside one mode: the selected row, or a tool the machine does not have. An
385	operation in flight is neither — it changes every tick, the row's spinner
386	already says so, and an entry that blinks says the opposite of the point.
387	
388	The mechanism lives in one place: `Shortcuts.ToStrings()` picks
389	`theme.ShortcutKeyDisabledStyle` (an alias of `ColorDim`, assigned in
390	`ApplyTheme` like the footer colours). The description is left alone — it is
391	already dim, so a disabled line reads as one uniform grey. `maxLenKey()` counts
392	the disabled entries, or the alignment would depend on availability and the
393	column would move anyway.
394	
395	**One calculation, two readers.** `shortcut.Availability` carries a single
396	`Reason string`, empty meaning available; `GetShortcuts` reads it to grey and
397	the handler reads it to refuse — so a greyed key that still acts is not
398	expressible, and the refusal cannot be silent. That silence is what it replaced:
399	`openInBrowser` returned `m, nil` on a repository with no remote, and `W` was
400	advertised anyway because the shortcut keyed on `IsGitRepo`. The reference
401	implementations are `internal/ui/workspaces/availability.go` and
402	`internal/ui/oci_resources/availability.go`.
403	
404	**A footer reason is for an action, not for a control.** `←→` on a field that is
405	not a cycle, `space` on what is not a checkbox, `tab` with one tab — greying is
406	the whole of it: there is nothing to explain, and a footer line on every stray
407	arrow key in a form would be noise.
408	
409	Two rules the entry earned:
410	
411	- **Not knowing is not knowing that not.** `scan.Detect` shells out,
412	  so it runs in the router's `Cmd` (`shared.ScanToolsMsg`) and `S`/`A` stay lit
413	  until it lands. Once it has, they are greyed on `Report.CanScan` — some tool
414	  ticked in an enabled category, applicable to the target, and there.
415	  Greying for three frames and un-greying reads as a fault — D20 at the scale of
416	  a key.
417	- **A key that applies whatever the row is stays out of the set.** `N` creates a
418	  directory in the *browsed* directory, so hiding it on a repository said "does
419	  not apply" about an action that worked; greying would repeat that, and
420	  refusing would be a regression.
421	
422	**Every view is migrated**, and what still replaces the list is the screen
423	changing: a mode, a tab, a state of the view, a signed-out screen — and, in the
424	viewer, the **document kind**. A Markdown file has no verbosity and never will,
425	which is a difference between openings rather than a "not now"; what varies
426	*within* one document — the tree against the text — is greyed like everything
427	else.
428	
429	Three things it turned up on the way through:
430	
431	- The Images tab advertised a **spinner frame as a key**: while a scan ran, `N`,
432	  `S` and `D` were replaced by an entry reading `󰑐  scanning...`, in the column
433	  that lists bindings. The row's own Scanned cell already carries that spinner
434	  (Rule 139). `TestNoShortcutAdvertisesAGlyphAsAKey` checks the Private Use
435	  Area rather than a list of icons, so nothing has to be kept in step with
436	  `theme/icons.go`.
437	- The **dashboard had no footer message** at all. It budgets an info line
438	  (Rule 124) and left it permanently empty, so `R` and `I` without a session
439	  fell through in silence with nowhere to say why.
440	- `R` **checked less than `I` did**: it opened a URL from a backend whose
441	  session was never verified. One `forgeLinks()` for both keys is what fixed it.
442	
443	## Multi-Context Configuration
444	
445	The app supports multiple configuration contexts (e.g., work, personal, client-A):
446	- Contexts are stored in `~/.devdesk/contexts/<name>/config.yaml`
447	- Current context is tracked in `~/.devdesk/current-context`
448	- Each context has isolated GitLab credentials via Git Credential Manager
449	- Context switching reinitializes all views with new config. While the switch
450	  loads (config, secret store, auto-login over the network) `switchingTo` is
451	  set: an overlay replaces the whole interface and only `ctrl+c` gets through,
452	  so the first views drawn afterwards are the new context's (D76)
453	
454	
455	## Shared State
456	
457	**A session is set and cleared by the router, both ways.** `setAuthenticated`
458	and `clearAuthenticated` in `internal/app/gitlab.go` are mirrors, and every
459	forge-backed view reads `sharedState` rather than holding its own answer. A
460	view resetting only its own fields is what D28 was: logging out left the client
461	and the user in place, so the explorer kept browsing and the header kept naming
462	a signed-out user.
463	
464	**`clearAuthenticated` is the only place a session is torn down.** Three sites
465	used to write the same three or four fields by hand — the secret-backend change,
466	the GitLab-URL change and the context switch — which is the shape D28 came in.
467	They call it now.
468	
469	**`IsAuthenticated` is the flag, and `Forge` is what you call.** The client used
470	to be both: `GitLabClient != nil` decided "is the user logged in" at three sites
471	while `IsAuthenticated` sat beside them saying the same thing. `CurrentUser` is
472	a value rather than a pointer for the same reason — a second way to ask a
473	question is how two answers come to disagree. The header shows the user when
474	there **is** a username, not when the flag is set, so a session whose user could
475	not be read does not print a bare `@`.
476	
477	Clearing `sharedState` does not empty a table a view already loaded, so a
478	session ending also drops the views — all but the one on screen that reported
479	it.
480	
481	
482	`internal/shared/state.go` holds cross-view data injected at view creation:
483	- `Secrets`, `SecretNotices` — the context's secret store and what the migration off plaintext reported
484	- `Forge`, `IsAuthenticated`, `CurrentUser` — the forge session (§3.6)
485	- `ForgeIndex *forgeindex.Index` — everything the session can see on the
486	  forge, at every depth, below. It is *not* the `CachedGroups`/`CachedProjects`
487	  D36 removed: those were never written; this one is written at every session
488	  start and never blocks anything
489	- `GitLabStats`, `DockerStats`, `OCIStats` — Dashboard counters. `GitLabStats`
490	  is a `*forge.DashboardStats`, whose five counters are each a `*int`: `nil`
491	  means nobody could read it, and the dashboard prints `-` rather than the `0`
492	  that read as "you have none" (D52)
493	- `ServiceStatus`, `ServiceComponents` — Status monitoring results
494	- `WorkspaceCount` — the dashboard's workspace counter
495	- `Tools *scan.Report` — the one detection of the scanners and the platform
496	  tools (§3.86), below
497	
498	### The scanners are detected once, by the router
499	
500	`internal/app/scan_tools.go`. `ws`, `oci`, `templates` and the dashboard used
501	to run a detection each — a LookPath and a `--version` per tool, a `docker
502	images` per tool in image mode, and four answers free to disagree. The router
503	now runs `scan.Detect` in a `Cmd` against a **copy** of `config.Scan.Tools`
504	(Rule 110), keeps the answer in `shared.State.Tools`, and hands it to every
505	view it holds as `shared.ScanToolsMsg` — `broadcastJobs`'s pattern, and
506	`createView` sends it to a view built afterwards.
507	
508	| Trigger | Where |
509	|---|---|
510	| start | `Init` |
511	| context switch | `handleContextSwitchComplete` — `forgetScanTools` first, so the new views say "not known yet" rather than show the old context's answer |
512	| a saved tool source, binary or image, or the engine | `handleConfigSaved` → `redetectIfToolsMoved`, comparing against the settings the last detection ran on (`scan.SameDetection`) — the configuration view edits the router's own `*config.Config`, so there is no "before" to compare to otherwise |
513	| `ctrl+r` on the dashboard | `shared.ScanToolsDetectRequestMsg` |
514	
515	**Not on a timer.** A tool is installed far less often than the dashboard
516	ticks; `ctrl+r` is the way to see one installed while DevDesk runs.
517	
518	**Every request is numbered** (`toolsGen`), and an answer that is not the latest
519	is dropped: a slow detection started before a source change would otherwise
520	land after the next one and put the old state back.
521	
522	**A category change does not re-detect.** What is *required* is worked out from
523	the configuration at read time (`scan.Required`, `Report.Missing(categories)`,
524	`Report.CanScan(categories, target)`); the report only says what is there.
525	
526	A scan runs on the same answer: each view sets `ScanOptions.Detected` where it
527	assembles its options, so `NewScanner` does not probe the machine again. A tool
528	that vanished in between fails at its stage, with the stage's own message.
529	
530	### The forge index is built once per session, by the router
531	
532	`internal/app/forge_index.go`, `internal/forgeindex`. The explorer's `g` needs
533	every path the session can see, and a drill-down is faster when the level is
534	already known — so the router builds one list for both, the way it detects the
535	scanners once for every view.
536	
537	| When | What |
538	|---|---|
539	| a session opens — auto-login, manual login, context switch (`setAuthenticated`) | the file the last walk left (`~/.devdesk/cache/forge/<context>.json`) is read at once; the walk waits for it |
540	| the file lands | installed, unless it was written for another host or account (`Index.Matches`) or a walk already landed. A walk starts as a job (`jobs.KindIndex`, cancellable in `:jobs`) only when the file cannot stand in for one (`forgeIndexNeedsWalk`): missing or not this account's, older than `forgeIndexMaxAge` (15 min), or carrying `Unlisted` namespaces — and not beside a walk already out. Leaving a context and coming back within minutes walks nothing (D77) |
541	| the walk lands | installed, written back to disk; a namespace whose listing failed is kept but marked unknown (`Unlisted`), and the run's detail says how many |
542	| a view edits it (`shared.ForgeIndexEditMsg`) | a create, a delete, a level re-read — the edit is a **function** applied to the router's current index. While a walk is out it is also kept (`forgeIndexPending`) and replayed on the walk's answer, which was read before it: a create or a delete confirmed during a walk is not undone when the walk lands. An edit that returns the same index (a level re-read unchanged, the common case) writes and broadcasts nothing |
543	| `ctrl+r` in the explorer (`shared.ForgeIndexRefreshMsg`) | a new walk, unless one is running; the index in place stays meanwhile |
544	| the session closes (`clearAuthenticated`) | the walk is cancelled, the index dropped; the file stays for the next session |
545	
546	**Every change is broadcast** as `shared.ForgeIndexChangedMsg` — no payload, the
547	index is on the shared state. **Answers are numbered** (`forgeIndexGen`) like the
548	scanners' detection, so a walk from a closed session cannot land in the next one.
549	
550	**The walk is undecorated.** No role, no CI status: on GitLab those cost two
551	requests per repository, and a pipeline status is stale within the minute. The
552	explorer decorates the level it shows (`docs/architecture/forge.md`).
553	
554	**An index is a value.** `With`, `Without` and `ReplaceLevel` return a new one:
555	the router hands the same index to a `Cmd` writing it to disk and to the views
556	reading it, and an in-place edit would race one against the other.
557	
558	## Cross-View Communication
559	
560	Key messages in `internal/app/messages.go`:
561	- `SwitchViewMsg` — navigate to another view
562	- `SelectionRequestMsg` / `SelectionResultMsg` — selection mode (e.g., workspaces opened from security view to pick a repo)
563	- `ImageScanResultLoadedMsg` / `WorkspaceScanResultLoadedMsg` — cached results ready
564	
565	### Long-running work reports without taking the screen
566	
567	A scan, a sync or a delete outlives the moment the user spends looking at the
568	view that started it. Its progress messages are therefore addressed **by name**
569	to that view — `routeToView(target, msg)` in `app.go` — and never to the view on
570	screen, and routing one never changes `currentView`.
571	
572	Three properties, and each is load-bearing:
573	
574	| | |
575	|---|---|
576	| The owning view is updated | it holds the row's marker, its footer state and its cache write; a message dropped because the user walked away leaves the row marked busy for the life of the view |
577	| The active view is *not* | it would act on progress that is not its own |
578	| `currentView` is untouched | `handleWorkspaceScanComplete` used to set it on every finished repository, so a batch of twelve made every other view unusable until the last one landed (D67) |
579	
580	The router does not re-measure the layout on these, unlike
581	`forwardToActiveView`: a view the user is not looking at cannot change the
582	footer's shape on screen, and it is measured on its way back in — `switchView`
583	asks for a resize.
584	
585	Making the marker survive re-entry is what makes the routing safe: `setEntries`
586	deliberately does not touch `scanningPaths`, so the reload `Init` triggers on
587	the way back in leaves in-flight work alone.
588	
589	### The jobs registry — `internal/jobs`
590	
591	One bookkeeping of everything long-running, owned by the router
592	(`App.jobs`). Before it there were four, and none could see the others:
593	`workspaces` kept three maps of paths, `oci_resources` a map of image names, the
594	security inventory a flag per row, and the clone screen five states per
595	repository. A scan started from `:sec` was therefore invisible to the `busy()`
596	guard in `ws`, and the two wrote the same cache entry.
597	
598	Two levels: a **`Run`** is one batch started in one go from one view, and holds
599	an **`Item`** per target. `RunState` is *derived* from the items and never
600	stored — a field would be a second answer to a question the items already
601	answer, and the two drift the first time a transition is missed.
602	
603	| | |
604	|---|---|
605	| `Start(run)` | admits a batch, from `Update` and never from a `Cmd` (Rule 110). Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what makes "8 waiting" sayable |
606	| `Advance(id, target, state, detail)` | one item moves. Returns false for work nobody registered, rather than swallowing it |
607	| `Attach` / `AttachRun` | store a `context.CancelFunc`; it arrives in the message that says the item started, because the context is created inside the `Cmd` |
608	| `Cancel(id)` | stops the queue always; cuts work in flight only where that leaves nothing behind (`Kind.Cancellable`) |
609	| `Snapshot()` | a **copy**, cancel functions cleared |
610	| `Running()` | runs that have not settled |
611	
612	`queued` and `running` are kept apart: the semaphore already knows the
613	difference and the clone screen already shows it, so collapsing them would make
614	that screen the only honest one.
615	
616	**A kind is not reserved for batches.** `create` and `delete` in the explorer
617	are single-item runs against a forge, and they are registered for the three
618	things the registry gives that a local flag does not: the spinner frame comes
619	from the broadcast rather than from a view's own chain — the explorer's stops on
620	`!m.loading`, so a frame taken from it would freeze the moment the tree settled;
621	the `busy()` guard sees work started anywhere; and `Run.Context` is stamped at
622	launch, so a create that outlives a context switch cannot write into the tree it
623	switched to. What decides is whether the work is a network call the user has to
624	be told about, not how many targets it has.
625	
626	`index` is the one kind no view starts: the router registers the forge walk
627	itself when a session opens (above). It is cancellable — the walk only reads,
628	and stopping it leaves the previous index in place.
629	
630	Runs live for the session, capped at the last `MaxFinishedRuns` settled ones; a
631	run still going is never pruned. Each is stamped with the context it started in,
632	and views **filter** (`jobs.FilterContext`) rather than the registry purging on a
633	switch — purging would contradict keeping them for the session.
634	
635	#### The stamp is what the work runs under
636	
637	A launch is two things and the router sequences them: it admits the run, then it
638	*builds* the work with the name it just stamped.
639	
640	```go
641	type StartMsg struct {
642		Run  Run
643		Work func(contextName string) tea.Cmd
644	}
645	```
646	
647	`Work` is a builder rather than a command because of D68. Stamping the run alone
648	left the registry telling the truth while every command of the batch read
649	`config.CurrentContextName()` for itself, minutes later — so a scan launched in
650	one context and finished in another wrote its counts into the cache of the
651	context the user had switched **to**. The builder is called once, in `Update`, so
652	the name is read once and every command of the launch shares the string.
653	
654	`jobs.Start` remains for work that does not depend on the context; a launch site
655	with no use for the name reads exactly as it did.
656	
657	What must carry the stamp is what **writes a result someone asked for under a
658	name** — a scan's counts, and the purge that clears them for it. What must not is
659	what *shows* the current context: a load (`loadScanCacheCmd`, `loadInventoryCmd`)
660	and a title both mean "current" by definition, and reading it is right there.
661	
662	#### An open run — the one whose targets arrive as it goes
663	
664	Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what
665	makes "8 waiting" sayable (D10). The clone does not: the walk that discovers
666	repositories *is* the slow part, so a run that waited for the list would show
667	nothing for the minutes that matter.
668	
669	`NewOpenRun` registers a run with no targets, and three methods carry it:
670	
671	| | |
672	|---|---|
673	| `Discover(kind, target, state, detail)` | appends a target, or advances one already there — the walk reports a group it could not list, and that path may also turn up as a repository |
674	| `Seal(kind)` | says the walk has found everything it is going to |
675	| `CancelOpen(kind)` | stops it, and seals — what would have closed the run is what was stopped |
676	
677	An open run is **never finished**, whatever its items say. `Transition.Discover`
678	is how a message asks for the first; `jobs.Sealer` is a second interface for the
679	second, because a closed channel names no target.
680	
681	All three name a **kind** rather than an identifier: a progressive run belongs
682	to a screen that owns the display while it goes, so there is one per kind at a
683	time and a view can name it without holding a `JobID` — the registry state D1
684	keeps out of views.
685	
686	#### Stopping work — the two halves of D7
687	
688	They are not the same question, and the key is offered on each independently:
689	
690	| | What it does | Offered when |
691	|---|---|---|
692	| `K` on a **run** (`Cancel`) | the queue stops — nothing further starts, whatever the kind; queued targets become `skipped: cancelled` | `Run.Stoppable()` |
693	| `K` on a **target** (`CancelItem`) | that one piece of work is cut | `Run.ItemStoppable(item)` — i.e. `Kind.Cancellable()` |
694	
695	`Run.Stoppable()` is the question about *this run*, not about its kind, and the
696	delete is the case it exists for: one item, in flight, of a kind that must never
697	be cut. `!Finished()` would offer the key and then refuse it, which is exactly
698	the silent refusal Rule 130 removes. The **create** answers the same way and for
699	a related reason — a request already sent cannot be un-sent, and a project whose
700	template is half applied is a state the forge holds, not one we can roll back.
701	
702	**A running target is asked to stop, never declared stopped.** It reports its
703	own outcome when it gets there; settling it here would race the message that
704	says how it actually ended. A *queued* one is skipped outright — it will not
705	run, and leaving it queued would keep the run reading as running forever.
706	
707	**The cancel travels on the transition that says the work started**
708	(`Transition.Cancel`). The context is created inside the `Cmd`, so it reaches
709	`Update` in that very message and the registry stores it in the same step that
710	marks the item running. Two steps would leave a window where the row spins and
711	the key does nothing — which is why `Attach` was folded into `Advance` and
712	removed.
713	
714	`CancelMsg` and `CancelItemMsg` name a `JobID`, where `CancelOpenMsg` names a
715	kind. The difference is which view is asking: a launch site cannot hold an
716	identifier — it would have to before the registry allocated one — but `:jobs`
717	reads it off the row it is rendering.
718	
719	### A progress message needs a case in the router
720	
721	A message reports to the registry by implementing `jobs.Reporter`, and the
722	registry hears it only when `routeWork` runs — which is called from a `case`
723	naming the message in `App.Update`. **Implementing the interface is not enough.**
724	A message with no case is still delivered to its view, which is what hides the
725	omission: the footer says the work finished while the registry keeps the run in
726	progress, and `:jobs` and the footer's status line show it running for the life
727	of the session. The scan and then the sync of the templates view each shipped
728	that way.
729	
730	`TestEveryJobReporterIsRoutedToTheRegistry` scans `internal/ui` for
731	`_ jobs.Reporter = X{}` declarations and fails naming any message the router has
732	no case for. Declare the compile-time proof next to the message, as the views
733	do, and the test finds it.
734	
735	### The broadcast, and the one spinner chain
736	
737	Views never hold a pointer to the registry. The router hands them a snapshot in
738	`jobs.ChangedMsg`, so nothing is read from `View()` while something else writes
739	it, and a view holding a snapshot cannot write back — every mutation goes
740	through the one owner.
741	
742	`broadcastJobs` updates **every held view**, on screen or not, so coming back to
743	one shows what happened while it was away without it having to ask; the layout
744	is re-measured once at the end, since only the view on screen can change the
745	footer's height. `sendJobsTo` covers the remaining case: a view built lazily on
746	the way in was there for none of it, so `switchView` hands it the snapshot.
747	
748	There is **one** spinner chain for the whole application, the router's
749	(`jobTickMsg`, `ensureJobTick`, `handleJobTick`). It is alive exactly while
750	`Running() > 0` and stops by not being renewed; a chain is identified by a
751	sequence number, so a tick from one already replaced is dropped and a second
752	chain is impossible rather than merely unlikely. The frame travels in the
753	message **bare** — Rule 122, because a view puts it in a table cell, which is
754	measured before it is styled — and `RenderedFrame()` is the styled reading a
755	footer takes (Rule 128).
756	
757	This is what removes the four hand-stamped frames, and with them the failure
758	each of them could produce: a chain that died on the first idle tick with
759	nothing able to restart it, leaving the spinner frozen on the frame it died at.
760	
761	
762	### The `:jobs` view — `internal/ui/jobsview`
763	
764	The reader's side of the registry, and it owns nothing: it starts no work, holds
765	no timer and fetches nothing. Its rows are the snapshot, so there is nothing to
766	refresh — `ctrl+r` is absent rather than greyed, because there is no operation
767	behind it to be unavailable.
768	
769	Two levels (D2): the runs, and `→` on one of them for its targets. A level
770	rather than a pair of tabs — the second table is *about* a row of the first, so
771	it is reached the way every drill-down in the application is (Rule 111), and the
772	trail is a breadcrumb below the table (Rule 123).
773	
774	| | Columns |
775	|---|---|
776	| runs | state glyph (untitled, `IconColumnWidth`), Kind, Label, Progress, State, Started |
777	| targets | state glyph, Target, State, Detail |
778	
779	**The first column is the state, not the kind**, and it is also where the
780	spinner goes — the containers table's shape. A jobs list is scanned to find the
781	run that failed and the one still going, so the glyph answers the question the
782	reader arrived with; the Kind column says in a word what sort of work it was,
783	and carries the state in its `Search` so `/failed` and `/scan` both work while
784	the glyph column stays out of the filter (Rule 125).
785	
786	A state glyph colours by the semantic status styles rather than by a
787	`theme.IconStyle` role. Roles exist for icons naming an *object* — a namespace, a
788	repository, an image — where the palette should be able to tell them apart; a
789	state already has a colour, and five new roles would give a theme five ways to
790	make `failed` not red.
791	
792	**The frame rides on the row.** `runRow`/`itemRow` wrap the model value with the
793	frame, because the columns are built once and close over nothing — the same
794	reason `oci_resources` has `imageRow`. It is the router's frame, taken bare from
795	`jobs.ChangedMsg`: using `datatable`'s own `AdvanceSpinner` here would be a
796	second chain beside the one D5 exists to keep single.
797	
798	**The context is passed, not read.** `jobsview.New(cfg, contextName)` takes the
799	name from the router, for D68's reason one screen over: the router is what knows
800	which context is current. The view filters the snapshot on it (`FilterContext`),
801	so a switch hides runs rather than dropping them — and the router rebuilds every
802	view on a switch anyway, so the cached name cannot go stale.
803	
804	`K` is state-aware at both levels (Rule 130) and greyed with a **named** reason:
805	"This run has already finished", "A delete cannot be stopped once it has
806	started". The refusal is never silent — pressing a greyed key says why in the
807	footer.
808	
809	**The dashboard gained the counter** the same way, and it is the one screen that
810	always gets D9's degraded form: it launches nothing, so it passes no origin, and
811	`2 jobs running — :jobs for details` is the whole of what it can honestly say.
812	The sentence itself is `components.JobsStatusLine`, shared with the workspaces
813	footer — two copies of a deliberate surrender would each have been free to
814	surrender differently.
815	
816	## Bubble Tea Message Flow
817	
818	Custom messages defined in view models (e.g., `internal/ui/status/model.go`):
819	```go
820	type TickMsg time.Time           // Countdown timer
821	type CheckStartedMsg struct{}    // Check initiated
822	type CheckCompleteMsg struct{}   // Check results ready
823	```
824

## A shortcut that does not apply is greyed, not dropped

`shortcut.Shortcut.Disabled` (§3.48). The entry keeps its place and the key
loses its colour and its weight, so the column no longer re-orders itself as the
cursor moves — which is what it is for: it is read out of the corner of the eye,
and a list that rearranges under the gaze cannot be.

**A mode still replaces the list.** A form has different keys from a table, so
greying them would show the union of every mode. What is greyed is a *state*
inside one mode: the selected row, or a tool the machine does not have. An
operation in flight is neither — it changes every tick, the row's spinner
already says so, and an entry that blinks says the opposite of the point.

The mechanism lives in one place: `Shortcuts.ToStrings()` picks
`theme.ShortcutKeyDisabledStyle` (an alias of `ColorDim`, assigned in
`ApplyTheme` like the footer colours). The description is left alone — it is
already dim, so a disabled line reads as one uniform grey. `maxLenKey()` counts
the disabled entries, or the alignment would depend on availability and the
column would move anyway.

**One calculation, two readers.** `shortcut.Availability` carries a single
`Reason string`, empty meaning available; `GetShortcuts` reads it to grey and
the handler reads it to refuse — so a greyed key that still acts is not
expressible, and the refusal cannot be silent. That silence is what it replaced:
`openInBrowser` returned `m, nil` on a repository with no remote, and `W` was
advertised anyway because the shortcut keyed on `IsGitRepo`. The reference
implementations are `internal/ui/workspaces/availability.go` and
`internal/ui/oci_resources/availability.go`.

**A footer reason is for an action, not for a control.** `←→` on a field that is
not a cycle, `space` on what is not a checkbox, `tab` with one tab — greying is
the whole of it: there is nothing to explain, and a footer line on every stray
arrow key in a form would be noise.

Two rules the entry earned:

- **Not knowing is not knowing that not.** `scan.Detect` shells out,
  so it runs in the router's `Cmd` (`shared.ScanToolsMsg`) and `S`/`A` stay lit
  until it lands. Once it has, they are greyed on `Report.CanScan` — some tool
  ticked in an enabled category, applicable to the target, and there.
  Greying for three frames and un-greying reads as a fault — D20 at the scale of
  a key.
- **A key that applies whatever the row is stays out of the set.** `N` creates a
  directory in the *browsed* directory, so hiding it on a repository said "does
  not apply" about an action that worked; greying would repeat that, and
  refusing would be a regression.

**Every view is migrated**, and what still replaces the list is the screen
changing: a mode, a tab, a state of the view, a signed-out screen — and, in the
viewer, the **document kind**. A Markdown file has no verbosity and never will,
which is a difference between openings rather than a "not now"; what varies
*within* one document — the tree against the text — is greyed like everything
else.

Three things it turned up on the way through:

- The Images tab advertised a **spinner frame as a key**: while a scan ran, `N`,
  `S` and `D` were replaced by an entry reading `󰑐  scanning...`, in the column
  that lists bindings. The row's own Scanned cell already carries that spinner
  (Rule 139). `TestNoShortcutAdvertisesAGlyphAsAKey` checks the Private Use
  Area rather than a list of icons, so nothing has to be kept in step with
  `theme/icons.go`.
- The **dashboard had no footer message** at all. It budgets an info line
  (Rule 124) and left it permanently empty, so `R` and `I` without a session
  fell through in silence with nowhere to say why.
- `R` **checked less than `I` did**: it opened a URL from a backend whose
  session was never verified. One `forgeLinks()` for both keys is what fixed it.

## Multi-Context Configuration

The app supports multiple configuration contexts (e.g., work, personal, client-A):
- Contexts are stored in `~/.devdesk/contexts/<name>/config.yaml`
- Current context is tracked in `~/.devdesk/current-context`
- Each context has isolated GitLab credentials via Git Credential Manager
- Context switching reinitializes all views with new config. While the switch
  loads (config, secret store, auto-login over the network) `switchingTo` is
  set: an overlay replaces the whole interface and only `ctrl+c` gets through,
  so the first views drawn afterwards are the new context's (D76)


## Shared State

**A session is set and cleared by the router, both ways.** `setAuthenticated`
and `clearAuthenticated` in `internal/app/gitlab.go` are mirrors, and every
forge-backed view reads `sharedState` rather than holding its own answer. A
view resetting only its own fields is what D28 was: logging out left the client
and the user in place, so the explorer kept browsing and the header kept naming
a signed-out user.

**`clearAuthenticated` is the only place a session is torn down.** Three sites
used to write the same three or four fields by hand — the secret-backend change,
the GitLab-URL change and the context switch — which is the shape D28 came in.
They call it now.

**`IsAuthenticated` is the flag, and `Forge` is what you call.** The client used
to be both: `GitLabClient != nil` decided "is the user logged in" at three sites
while `IsAuthenticated` sat beside them saying the same thing. `CurrentUser` is
a value rather than a pointer for the same reason — a second way to ask a
question is how two answers come to disagree. The header shows the user when
there **is** a username, not when the flag is set, so a session whose user could
not be read does not print a bare `@`.

Clearing `sharedState` does not empty a table a view already loaded, so a
session ending also drops the views — all but the one on screen that reported
it.


`internal/shared/state.go` holds cross-view data injected at view creation:
- `Secrets`, `SecretNotices` — the context's secret store and what the migration off plaintext reported
- `Forge`, `IsAuthenticated`, `CurrentUser` — the forge session (§3.6)
- `ForgeIndex *forgeindex.Index` — everything the session can see on the
  forge, at every depth, below. It is *not* the `CachedGroups`/`CachedProjects`
  D36 removed: those were never written; this one is written at every session
  start and never blocks anything
- `GitLabStats`, `DockerStats`, `OCIStats` — Dashboard counters. `GitLabStats`
  is a `*forge.DashboardStats`, whose five counters are each a `*int`: `nil`
  means nobody could read it, and the dashboard prints `-` rather than the `0`
  that read as "you have none" (D52)
- `ServiceStatus`, `ServiceComponents` — Status monitoring results
- `WorkspaceCount` — the dashboard's workspace counter
- `Tools *scan.Report` — the one detection of the scanners and the platform
  tools (§3.86), below

### The scanners are detected once, by the router

`internal/app/scan_tools.go`. `ws`, `oci`, `templates` and the dashboard used
to run a detection each — a LookPath and a `--version` per tool, a `docker
images` per tool in image mode, and four answers free to disagree. The router
now runs `scan.Detect` in a `Cmd` against a **copy** of `config.Scan.Tools`
(Rule 110), keeps the answer in `shared.State.Tools`, and hands it to every
view it holds as `shared.ScanToolsMsg` — `broadcastJobs`'s pattern, and
`createView` sends it to a view built afterwards.

| Trigger | Where |
|---|---|
| start | `Init` |
| context switch | `handleContextSwitchComplete` — `forgetScanTools` first, so the new views say "not known yet" rather than show the old context's answer |
| a saved tool source, binary or image, or the engine | `handleConfigSaved` → `redetectIfToolsMoved`, comparing against the settings the last detection ran on (`scan.SameDetection`) — the configuration view edits the router's own `*config.Config`, so there is no "before" to compare to otherwise |
| `ctrl+r` on the dashboard | `shared.ScanToolsDetectRequestMsg` |

**Not on a timer.** A tool is installed far less often than the dashboard
ticks; `ctrl+r` is the way to see one installed while DevDesk runs.

**Every request is numbered** (`toolsGen`), and an answer that is not the latest
is dropped: a slow detection started before a source change would otherwise
land after the next one and put the old state back.

**A category change does not re-detect.** What is *required* is worked out from
the configuration at read time (`scan.Required`, `Report.Missing(categories)`,
`Report.CanScan(categories, target)`); the report only says what is there.

A scan runs on the same answer: each view sets `ScanOptions.Detected` where it
assembles its options, so `NewScanner` does not probe the machine again. A tool
that vanished in between fails at its stage, with the stage's own message.

### The forge index is built once per session, by the router

`internal/app/forge_index.go`, `internal/forgeindex`. The explorer's `g` needs
every path the session can see, and a drill-down is faster when the level is
already known — so the router builds one list for both, the way it detects the
scanners once for every view.

| When | What |
|---|---|
| a session opens — auto-login, manual login, context switch (`setAuthenticated`) | the file the last walk left (`~/.devdesk/cache/forge/<context>.json`) is read at once; the walk waits for it |
| the file lands | installed, unless it was written for another host or account (`Index.Matches`) or a walk already landed. A walk starts as a job (`jobs.KindIndex`, cancellable in `:jobs`) only when the file cannot stand in for one (`forgeIndexNeedsWalk`): missing or not this account's, older than `forgeIndexMaxAge` (15 min), or carrying `Unlisted` namespaces — and not beside a walk already out. Leaving a context and coming back within minutes walks nothing (D77) |
| the walk lands | installed, written back to disk; a namespace whose listing failed is kept but marked unknown (`Unlisted`), and the run's detail says how many |
| a view edits it (`shared.ForgeIndexEditMsg`) | a create, a delete, a level re-read — the edit is a **function** applied to the router's current index. While a walk is out it is also kept (`forgeIndexPending`) and replayed on the walk's answer, which was read before it: a create or a delete confirmed during a walk is not undone when the walk lands. An edit that returns the same index (a level re-read unchanged, the common case) writes and broadcasts nothing |
| `ctrl+r` in the explorer (`shared.ForgeIndexRefreshMsg`) | a new walk, unless one is running; the index in place stays meanwhile |
| the session closes (`clearAuthenticated`) | the walk is cancelled, the index dropped; the file stays for the next session |

**Every change is broadcast** as `shared.ForgeIndexChangedMsg` — no payload, the
index is on the shared state. **Answers are numbered** (`forgeIndexGen`) like the
scanners' detection, so a walk from a closed session cannot land in the next one.

**The walk is undecorated.** No role, no CI status: on GitLab those cost two
requests per repository, and a pipeline status is stale within the minute. The
explorer decorates the level it shows (`docs/architecture/forge.md`).

**An index is a value.** `With`, `Without` and `ReplaceLevel` return a new one:
the router hands the same index to a `Cmd` writing it to disk and to the views
reading it, and an in-place edit would race one against the other.

## Cross-View Communication

Key messages in `internal/app/messages.go`:
- `SwitchViewMsg` — navigate to another view
- `SelectionRequestMsg` / `SelectionResultMsg` — selection mode (e.g., workspaces opened from security view to pick a repo)
- `ImageScanResultLoadedMsg` / `WorkspaceScanResultLoadedMsg` — cached results ready

### Long-running work reports without taking the screen

A scan, a sync or a delete outlives the moment the user spends looking at the
view that started it. Its progress messages are therefore addressed **by name**
to that view — `routeToView(target, msg)` in `app.go` — and never to the view on
screen, and routing one never changes `currentView`.

Three properties, and each is load-bearing:

| | |
|---|---|
| The owning view is updated | it holds the row's marker, its footer state and its cache write; a message dropped because the user walked away leaves the row marked busy for the life of the view |
| The active view is *not* | it would act on progress that is not its own |
| `currentView` is untouched | `handleWorkspaceScanComplete` used to set it on every finished repository, so a batch of twelve made every other view unusable until the last one landed (D67) |

The router does not re-measure the layout on these, unlike
`forwardToActiveView`: a view the user is not looking at cannot change the
footer's shape on screen, and it is measured on its way back in — `switchView`
asks for a resize.

Making the marker survive re-entry is what makes the routing safe: `setEntries`
deliberately does not touch `scanningPaths`, so the reload `Init` triggers on
the way back in leaves in-flight work alone.

### The jobs registry — `internal/jobs`

One bookkeeping of everything long-running, owned by the router
(`App.jobs`). Before it there were four, and none could see the others:
`workspaces` kept three maps of paths, `oci_resources` a map of image names, the
security inventory a flag per row, and the clone screen five states per
repository. A scan started from `:sec` was therefore invisible to the `busy()`
guard in `ws`, and the two wrote the same cache entry.

Two levels: a **`Run`** is one batch started in one go from one view, and holds
an **`Item`** per target. `RunState` is *derived* from the items and never
stored — a field would be a second answer to a question the items already
answer, and the two drift the first time a transition is missed.

| | |
|---|---|
| `Start(run)` | admits a batch, from `Update` and never from a `Cmd` (Rule 110). Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what makes "8 waiting" sayable |
| `Advance(id, target, state, detail)` | one item moves. Returns false for work nobody registered, rather than swallowing it |
| `Attach` / `AttachRun` | store a `context.CancelFunc`; it arrives in the message that says the item started, because the context is created inside the `Cmd` |
| `Cancel(id)` | stops the queue always; cuts work in flight only where that leaves nothing behind (`Kind.Cancellable`) |
| `Snapshot()` | a **copy**, cancel functions cleared |
| `Running()` | runs that have not settled |

`queued` and `running` are kept apart: the semaphore already knows the
difference and the clone screen already shows it, so collapsing them would make
that screen the only honest one.

**A kind is not reserved for batches.** `create` and `delete` in the explorer
are single-item runs against a forge, and they are registered for the three
things the registry gives that a local flag does not: the spinner frame comes
from the broadcast rather than from a view's own chain — the explorer's stops on
`!m.loading`, so a frame taken from it would freeze the moment the tree settled;
the `busy()` guard sees work started anywhere; and `Run.Context` is stamped at
launch, so a create that outlives a context switch cannot write into the tree it
switched to. What decides is whether the work is a network call the user has to
be told about, not how many targets it has.

`index` is the one kind no view starts: the router registers the forge walk
itself when a session opens (above). It is cancellable — the walk only reads,
and stopping it leaves the previous index in place.

Runs live for the session, capped at the last `MaxFinishedRuns` settled ones; a
run still going is never pruned. Each is stamped with the context it started in,
and views **filter** (`jobs.FilterContext`) rather than the registry purging on a
switch — purging would contradict keeping them for the session.

#### The stamp is what the work runs under

A launch is two things and the router sequences them: it admits the run, then it
*builds* the work with the name it just stamped.

```go
type StartMsg struct {
	Run  Run
	Work func(contextName string) tea.Cmd
}
```

`Work` is a builder rather than a command because of D68. Stamping the run alone
left the registry telling the truth while every command of the batch read
`config.CurrentContextName()` for itself, minutes later — so a scan launched in
one context and finished in another wrote its counts into the cache of the
context the user had switched **to**. The builder is called once, in `Update`, so
the name is read once and every command of the launch shares the string.

`jobs.Start` remains for work that does not depend on the context; a launch site
with no use for the name reads exactly as it did.

What must carry the stamp is what **writes a result someone asked for under a
name** — a scan's counts, and the purge that clears them for it. What must not is
what *shows* the current context: a load (`loadScanCacheCmd`, `loadInventoryCmd`)
and a title both mean "current" by definition, and reading it is right there.

#### An open run — the one whose targets arrive as it goes

Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what
makes "8 waiting" sayable (D10). The clone does not: the walk that discovers
repositories *is* the slow part, so a run that waited for the list would show
nothing for the minutes that matter.

`NewOpenRun` registers a run with no targets, and three methods carry it:

| | |
|---|---|
| `Discover(kind, target, state, detail)` | appends a target, or advances one already there — the walk reports a group it could not list, and that path may also turn up as a repository |
| `Seal(kind)` | says the walk has found everything it is going to |
| `CancelOpen(kind)` | stops it, and seals — what would have closed the run is what was stopped |

An open run is **never finished**, whatever its items say. `Transition.Discover`
is how a message asks for the first; `jobs.Sealer` is a second interface for the
second, because a closed channel names no target.

All three name a **kind** rather than an identifier: a progressive run belongs
to a screen that owns the display while it goes, so there is one per kind at a
time and a view can name it without holding a `JobID` — the registry state D1
keeps out of views.

#### Stopping work — the two halves of D7

They are not the same question, and the key is offered on each independently:

| | What it does | Offered when |
|---|---|---|
| `K` on a **run** (`Cancel`) | the queue stops — nothing further starts, whatever the kind; queued targets become `skipped: cancelled` | `Run.Stoppable()` |
| `K` on a **target** (`CancelItem`) | that one piece of work is cut | `Run.ItemStoppable(item)` — i.e. `Kind.Cancellable()` |

`Run.Stoppable()` is the question about *this run*, not about its kind, and the
delete is the case it exists for: one item, in flight, of a kind that must never
be cut. `!Finished()` would offer the key and then refuse it, which is exactly
the silent refusal Rule 130 removes. The **create** answers the same way and for
a related reason — a request already sent cannot be un-sent, and a project whose
template is half applied is a state the forge holds, not one we can roll back.

**A running target is asked to stop, never declared stopped.** It reports its
own outcome when it gets there; settling it here would race the message that
says how it actually ended. A *queued* one is skipped outright — it will not
run, and leaving it queued would keep the run reading as running forever.

**The cancel travels on the transition that says the work started**
(`Transition.Cancel`). The context is created inside the `Cmd`, so it reaches
`Update` in that very message and the registry stores it in the same step that
marks the item running. Two steps would leave a window where the row spins and
the key does nothing — which is why `Attach` was folded into `Advance` and
removed.

`CancelMsg` and `CancelItemMsg` name a `JobID`, where `CancelOpenMsg` names a
kind. The difference is which view is asking: a launch site cannot hold an
identifier — it would have to before the registry allocated one — but `:jobs`
reads it off the row it is rendering.

### A progress message needs a case in the router

A message reports to the registry by implementing `jobs.Reporter`, and the
registry hears it only when `routeWork` runs — which is called from a `case`
naming the message in `App.Update`. **Implementing the interface is not enough.**
A message with no case is still delivered to its view, which is what hides the
omission: the footer says the work finished while the registry keeps the run in
progress, and `:jobs` and the footer's status line show it running for the life
of the session. The scan and then the sync of the templates view each shipped
that way.

`TestEveryJobReporterIsRoutedToTheRegistry` scans `internal/ui` for
`_ jobs.Reporter = X{}` declarations and fails naming any message the router has
no case for. Declare the compile-time proof next to the message, as the views
do, and the test finds it.

### The broadcast, and the one spinner chain

Views never hold a pointer to the registry. The router hands them a snapshot in
`jobs.ChangedMsg`, so nothing is read from `View()` while something else writes
it, and a view holding a snapshot cannot write back — every mutation goes
through the one owner.

`broadcastJobs` updates **every held view**, on screen or not, so coming back to
one shows what happened while it was away without it having to ask; the layout
is re-measured once at the end, since only the view on screen can change the
footer's height. `sendJobsTo` covers the remaining case: a view built lazily on
the way in was there for none of it, so `switchView` hands it the snapshot.

There is **one** spinner chain for the whole application, the router's
(`jobTickMsg`, `ensureJobTick`, `handleJobTick`). It is alive exactly while
`Running() > 0` and stops by not being renewed; a chain is identified by a
sequence number, so a tick from one already replaced is dropped and a second
chain is impossible rather than merely unlikely. The frame travels in the
message **bare** — Rule 122, because a view puts it in a table cell, which is
measured before it is styled — and `RenderedFrame()` is the styled reading a
footer takes (Rule 128).

This is what removes the four hand-stamped frames, and with them the failure
each of them could produce: a chain that died on the first idle tick with
nothing able to restart it, leaving the spinner frozen on the frame it died at.


### The `:jobs` view — `internal/ui/jobsview`

The reader's side of the registry, and it owns nothing: it starts no work, holds
no timer and fetches nothing. Its rows are the snapshot, so there is nothing to
refresh — `ctrl+r` is absent rather than greyed, because there is no operation
behind it to be unavailable.

Two levels (D2): the runs, and `→` on one of them for its targets. A level
rather than a pair of tabs — the second table is *about* a row of the first, so
it is reached the way every drill-down in the application is (Rule 111), and the
trail is a breadcrumb below the table (Rule 123).

| | Columns |
|---|---|
| runs | state glyph (untitled, `IconColumnWidth`), Kind, Label, Progress, State, Started |
| targets | state glyph, Target, State, Detail |

**The first column is the state, not the kind**, and it is also where the
spinner goes — the containers table's shape. A jobs list is scanned to find the
run that failed and the one still going, so the glyph answers the question the
reader arrived with; the Kind column says in a word what sort of work it was,
and carries the state in its `Search` so `/failed` and `/scan` both work while
the glyph column stays out of the filter (Rule 125).

A state glyph colours by the semantic status styles rather than by a
`theme.IconStyle` role. Roles exist for icons naming an *object* — a namespace, a
repository, an image — where the palette should be able to tell them apart; a
state already has a colour, and five new roles would give a theme five ways to
make `failed` not red.

**The frame rides on the row.** `runRow`/`itemRow` wrap the model value with the
frame, because the columns are built once and close over nothing — the same
reason `oci_resources` has `imageRow`. It is the router's frame, taken bare from
`jobs.ChangedMsg`: using `datatable`'s own `AdvanceSpinner` here would be a
second chain beside the one D5 exists to keep single.

**The context is passed, not read.** `jobsview.New(cfg, contextName)` takes the
name from the router, for D68's reason one screen over: the router is what knows
which context is current. The view filters the snapshot on it (`FilterContext`),
so a switch hides runs rather than dropping them — and the router rebuilds every
view on a switch anyway, so the cached name cannot go stale.

`K` is state-aware at both levels (Rule 130) and greyed with a **named** reason:
"This run has already finished", "A delete cannot be stopped once it has
started". The refusal is never silent — pressing a greyed key says why in the
footer.

**The dashboard gained the counter** the same way, and it is the one screen that
always gets D9's degraded form: it launches nothing, so it passes no origin, and
`2 jobs running — :jobs for details` is the whole of what it can honestly say.
The sentence itself is `components.JobsStatusLine`, shared with the workspaces
footer — two copies of a deliberate surrender would each have been free to
surrender differently.

## Bubble Tea Message Flow

Custom messages defined in view models (e.g., `internal/ui/status/model.go`):
```go
type TickMsg time.Time           // Countdown timer
type CheckStartedMsg struct{}    // Check initiated
type CheckCompleteMsg struct{}   // Check results ready
```

9	// StartMsg asks the router to register a run and then dispatch the work that
10	// fills it.
11	//
12	// The view builds the run — it is the only place that knows the targets — and
13	// the router admits it, stamps it with the current context and starts the work
14	// (D10). Registration happens in Update, never inside a Cmd (Rule 110).
15	//
16	// Work rides on the message rather than being batched beside it because the
17	// order matters: a transition naming a run the registry has not admitted yet is
18	// refused, and a tea.Batch gives no order. The router is the sequencer, which
19	// is a smaller thing to get right than a Sequence at every launch site — and it
20	// leaves the work runnable only by the router, so a test can read what was
21	// launched without launching it.
22	type StartMsg struct {
23		Run Run
24	
25		// Work is a builder rather than a command because the context is stamped
26		// by the router, one step after the view has described the run (D8). Work
27		// that writes into a context-scoped cache needs that name, and reading it
28		// back from the configuration inside the command is the defect the stamp
29		// exists to close: a batch outliving a context switch wrote its last
30		// results into the cache of the context it had switched to.
31		//
32		// It is never nil for a run with work: Start passes a builder that ignores
33		// the name, so a launch site that has no use for it reads as it did.
34		Work func(contextName string) tea.Cmd
35	
36		// Cancel stops the run's queue, and is nil for the kinds that have nothing
37		// to stop. It travels here rather than arriving later like an item's cancel
38		// because a progressive run owns its context from the launch: the pipeline
39		// is started in Update, so the function exists before the run is admitted.
40		Cancel context.CancelFunc
41	
42		// Invocation names the MCP call that asked for this run, and is empty when
43		// a person pressed a key (§3.61).
44		//
45		// It travels on the message rather than being matched by time: a router
46		// that remembered "an invocation is in flight" and gave its identifier to
47		// the next StartMsg would have a window of one Update cycle, in which a
48		// keypress can land — and the agent would be handed the identifier of the
49		// scan the user just started by hand. It is the shape of Run.Context: a
50		// fact carried by what it is about, decided once.
51		Invocation string
52	}
53	
54	// WithInvocation stamps the run a jobs.Start* command is about to register with
55	// the call that asked for it.
56	//
57	// A decorator rather than a fourth constructor: Start, StartInContext and
58	// StartCancellable already differ along two axes, and an invocation-carrying
59	// variant of each would be six. A view's MCP handler wraps the command it was
60	// already returning, at the one place that knows who asked.
61	//
62	// An empty invocation returns the command untouched, so a keyboard launch pays
63	// nothing and reads as it did.
64	func WithInvocation(invocation string, cmd tea.Cmd) tea.Cmd {
65		if invocation == "" || cmd == nil {
66			return cmd
67		}
68		return func() tea.Msg {
69			msg := cmd()
70			start, ok := msg.(StartMsg)
71			if !ok {
72				return msg
73			}
74			start.Invocation = invocation
75			return start
76		}
77	}

79	// RefusedMsg says an invocation will not produce a run, and why.
80	//
81	// It is the sibling of StartMsg and lives beside it for that reason: between
82	// them they are everything an invocation can come to. A keypress needs no such
83	// message — the view puts the same sentence in its footer (Rule 130) — which is
84	// why Refuse returns nil for an empty invocation rather than a message nobody
85	// would route.
86	//
87	// Reason is the view's own Availability.Reason, so the sentence an agent reads
88	// is the one the header greys with and the footer prints. One calculation,
89	// three readers.
90	type RefusedMsg struct {
91		Invocation string
92		Reason     string
93	}
94	
95	// Refuse builds the message, or nothing at all for a keyboard launch.
96	func Refuse(invocation, reason string) tea.Cmd {
97		if invocation == "" {
98			return nil
99		}
100		return func() tea.Msg {
101			return RefusedMsg{Invocation: invocation, Reason: reason}
102		}
103	}

105	// Start builds the message for work that does not depend on the context.
106	func Start(run Run, work tea.Cmd) tea.Cmd {
107		return StartInContext(run, func(string) tea.Cmd { return work })

111	// today the clone, whose pipeline is launched from Update and hands back its
112	// context there and then.
113	func StartCancellable(run Run, work tea.Cmd, cancel context.CancelFunc) tea.Cmd {
114		return func() tea.Msg {
115			return StartMsg{
116				Run:    run,
117				Work:   func(string) tea.Cmd { return work },
118				Cancel: cancel,
119			}
120		}
121	}

128	// views.

130		Kind Kind

136	}

164	// StartInContext builds the message for work that writes into a context-scoped

167	// long the batch runs.

172	// ChangedMsg carries what the registry holds to every view that might show it.
173	// It is the whole of the broadcast (D1): a view keeps its own copy of a
174	// snapshot rather than reading a pointer the router writes, so nothing is read
175	// from View() while something else is writing it.
176	//
177	// It is sent on two occasions, and they are different in nature: a transition —
178	// something actually happened — and a spinner tick, where only the frame moved.
179	// The receiver does not have to tell them apart, which is why there is one
180	// message and not two.
181	//

183	// name it without importing the router, which imports them.
184	type ChangedMsg struct {
185		// Runs is a copy, oldest first, every context included. Filtering on the
186		// current one is the view's business (D8, FilterContext).
187		Runs []Run
188	
189		// Frame is the current spinner frame, bare — no escape sequence. Rule 122:
190		// a table cell is measured before it is styled, so a styled frame of seven
191		// visible cells measures twenty-eight and is truncated inside its own
192		// escape, which then bleeds down the rest of the table.
193		Frame string
194	
195		// RenderedFrame is the same frame styled, which is what a footer takes
196		// (Rule 128 — measurement there goes through lipgloss.Width, which ignores
197		// escapes). The router fills both so the two readings of one frame cannot
198		// drift, and so this package needs to know nothing about styling.
199		RenderedFrame string
200	}
201	
202	// Running counts the runs in the snapshot that have not settled. It saves every
203	// receiver the same three lines.
204	func (m ChangedMsg) Running() int {
205		return len(Unfinished(m.Runs))
206	}

27	// handleStartJobs admits a run a view built and asks the registry for it.
28	//
29	// The context is stamped here rather than by the view: the router is what knows
30	// which context is current, and a view reading it back from the configuration
31	// would be reading it again — which is the shape of the defect the stamp exists
32	// to close (a batch outliving a switch and writing into the new context's
33	// cache).
34	//
35	// The stamp is then handed to the work, which is the half that was missing
36	// (D68): a run carrying the right name while its commands re-read the current
37	// one told `:jobs` the truth and wrote the cache anyway. Building the work here
38	// means the name is read once, in Update, and every command of the batch shares
39	// the string — a switch three repositories later cannot reach it.
40	func (a *App) handleStartJobs(msg jobs.StartMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
41		run := msg.Run
42		run.Context = a.currentContext
43		id := a.jobs.Start(run)
44		if msg.Cancel != nil {
45			a.jobs.AttachRun(id, msg.Cancel)
46		}

48		// waiting for one is answered from this handler (§3.61).
49		a.settleInvocation(msg.Invocation, id, nil)
50		// The work goes out after the registration, which is the whole reason it
51		// travels on the message: a transition naming a run the registry has not
52		// admitted yet is refused, and the row would spin for the life of the view.
53		cmds := []tea.Cmd{a.jobsChanged()}
54		if msg.Work != nil {
55			cmds = append(cmds, msg.Work(run.Context))
56		}
57		return a, tea.Batch(cmds...)
58	}

60	// routeWork applies a progress message to the registry and hands it to the view
61	// that owns it.

64	// reading a current snapshot when it handles it — which is what lets it ask
65	// "has my batch finished?" rather than counting alongside.

68	// has its own reasons to see it, and Apply already returned false rather than
69	// inventing a run for it.

71		var cmds []tea.Cmd
72		if reporter, ok := msg.(jobs.Reporter); ok {
73			if a.jobs.Apply(reporter.Transition()) {
74				cmds = append(cmds, a.jobsChanged())
75			}
76		}
77		// A sealer says a progressive run has found everything it is going to
78		// (D3). It is a second interface because sealing names no target — the
79		// message carrying it is a closed channel, and there is nothing for it to
80		// be about.

82			if a.jobs.Seal(sealer.Seal()) {
83				cmds = append(cmds, a.jobsChanged())
84			}
85		}
